pedagogy.summary:
• Age/Topic — Sexual Selection, Kin Selection & Game Theory (ages 12–13): sexual selection as a form of natural selection acting on mating success (runaway selection for peacock tails, bird-of-paradise displays, frog calls), kin selection and altruism (worker bees, meerkat sentinels) via Hamilton's rule and inclusive fitness, game theory in behaviour (hawk-dove/ESS), and cognitive ethology (evidence for animal emotion, play, culture).
• Standards — UK (DfE KS3): extends natural selection and variation into WHY apparently costly or self-sacrificing traits evolve; a working-scientifically strand on constructing evidence-based explanations of behaviour.
• Standards — US (NGSS): MS-LS4-4 (natural selection and differential reproductive success); HS-LS4 horizon; complements MS-LS2-2 interactions — here selection acts through mating and kinship.
• Operational details: the unifying move is that fitness = REPRODUCTIVE success, so a trait that lowers survival can still spread if it raises mating success (peacock tail) or if it helps copies of one's genes in relatives (Hamilton's rule: rB > C). Teach sexual selection (female choice / male-male competition; runaway and handicap/honest-signal ideas), kin selection/inclusive fitness (why sterile workers and self-endangering sentinels evolve), and game theory (hawk-dove, evolutionarily stable strategy — the best move depends on what everyone else does). Touch cognitive ethology carefully as an evidence question. Resolve the apparent paradox 'why would evolution favour a costly tail or self-sacrifice?'.
• Checkpoint — A (concrete, ~12): explain how a costly ornament like a peacock's tail can be favoured (mating advantage). B (transitional, ~12–13): state Hamilton's rule in words and use it to explain altruism toward relatives. C (formal, ~13): explain an evolutionarily stable strategy with the hawk-dove game — why the best behaviour depends on the frequency of others' strategies.
bestPractices: Redefine fitness explicitly as reproductive success (not survival or strength), so the peacock's survival-costly tail stops being paradoxical.
Teach Hamilton's rule (rB > C) with worked relatedness numbers (helping a full sibling, r=0.5) so altruism becomes a quantitative gene's-eye prediction, not a vague 'for the good of the group'.
Use the hawk-dove game with payoffs the student can compute so an evolutionarily stable strategy emerges as frequency-dependent — the best move depends on what everyone else does.
Actively dismantle 'for the good of the species' group-selection thinking, replacing it with individual/gene-level reasoning.
keyRepresentations: A female-choice / handicap diagram: ornament size vs both survival cost and mating benefit, with the net-fitness optimum.
A relatedness tree with r-values annotated, feeding Hamilton's rule rB > C.
A hawk-dove payoff matrix with a frequency slider showing the stable mix (ESS).
A 'fitness = reproductive success' concept map linking survival, mating, and helping relatives to gene copies in the next generation.
commonMisconceptions: 'Animals do things for the good of the species/group' — selection favours traits raising the individual's (or its genes') reproductive success; group-selection explanations are usually wrong.
'The fittest = the strongest or longest-lived' — fitness is reproductive success; a short-lived, showy male can be fitter than a drab survivor.
'Costly ornaments are just decoration with no function' — they can be honest signals of quality or products of runaway female choice.
'Altruism disproves natural selection / animals are just being nice' — kin selection (helping relatives who share genes) explains apparent self-sacrifice quantitatively.
'There's always one single best behaviour' — the best strategy can be frequency-dependent (an ESS is a mix, not a lone winner).

learn.summary: Learners explore why apparently costly or self-sacrificing traits evolve by redefining fitness as reproductive success. Three linked models drive the ideas: a sexual-selection trade-off (ornament cost vs mating benefit), Hamilton's rule for kin-selected altruism (rB > C), and the hawk-dove game showing a frequency-dependent evolutionarily stable strategy. A concept check and an optional debate extension cover the definition of fitness, computing rB vs C, reading payoff matrices, and the evidence question of cognitive ethology.

activities.title: Peacock's tail: when a survival cost pays off
feedback: If a learner predicts the tail should disappear because it only hurts survival: they are treating survival as the whole of fitness. Point to the mating-success curve — more offspring from showier males can outweigh the survival cost.

If a learner says the peacock grows a big tail 'on purpose' to look good: recast it as selection over many generations on heritable variation in tail size via peahen preference, not a choice made within one individual's lifetime.
If a learner picks the smallest tail as 'best': ask them to read the NET curve, not the survival curve alone — the fitness optimum is where mating benefit minus survival cost is greatest.
activities.rationale: Making the two competing curves manipulable lets the paradox dissolve through the learner's own trade-off reasoning rather than assertion; a live female-preference control connects runaway selection to the shifting optimum. A labelled static ornament diagram can introduce the trade-off but cannot let learners locate the net-fitness peak by adjusting the variables.
sourceClaims: Sexual selection (female choice, male-male competition, runaway and handicap/honest-signal models) explains costly ornaments; kin selection via Hamilton's rule (rB > C) and inclusive fitness explains altruism toward relatives.
Natural selection acts through differential reproductive success and changes trait distributions over generations.
learnerActions: Vary the size of a peacock's ornament and read off two quantities that change with it: a rising survival cost (slower, easier for predators to catch) and a rising mating success (peahens choose showier males).

Combine the two into a net reproductive-success curve and find where it peaks. With the model's settings, notice the peak can sit at a large, 'wasteful'-looking tail rather than a small survival-safe one.

Increase the strength of female preference and observe how the optimum tail size shifts larger. In runaway selection, the preference and the tail evolve together over generations because offspring inherit both, so this pressure can keep strengthening.

Relate the same cost-versus-mating trade-off to other sexually selected traits — bird-of-paradise courtship displays and loud frog mating calls — and note that the mating advantage can arise through female choice OR through male-male competition.
State in your own words why natural selection has NOT removed the costly tail.
activities.intendedInsight: Fitness means reproductive success, not survival or strength: a trait that lowers survival can still spread if it raises mating success enough. The same logic covers other sexually selected traits (bird-of-paradise displays, frog calls) and both routes to mating success — female choice and male-male competition. Ornaments can be honest signals of quality or products of runaway female choice, not mere decoration.

activities.title: Hamilton's rule: why a sterile worker or a sentinel helps
feedback: If a learner explains the worker bee's sacrifice as 'for the good of the species': introduce inclusive fitness — helping close relatives propagates shared genes, so the sacrifice favours copies of the helper's own genes carried in kin.
If a learner uses r for distant kin as if it were 0.5: have them check the relatedness value; the lower r shrinks rB and raises the bar for helping to pay off.
If a learner concludes altruism disproves natural selection: show that the rule PREDICTS when helping is favoured, so apparent niceness is consistent with gene-level selection.
activities.rationale: Letting learners set r, B and C and watch the rB-versus-C threshold decide the gene's fate turns altruism into a quantitative prediction with worked relatedness numbers, directly targeting the group-selection misconception. A written statement of the rule alone leaves the threshold abstract.
sourceClaims: Sexual selection (female choice, male-male competition, runaway and handicap/honest-signal models) explains costly ornaments; kin selection via Hamilton's rule (rB > C) and inclusive fitness explains altruism toward relatives.
KS3 natural selection and variation provide the basis for explaining why costly or self-sacrificing traits evolve.
learnerActions: Set a relatedness value r for the helper and the helped (e.g. full sibling r = 0.5), a benefit B to the relative, and a cost C to the helper.
Compute rB and compare it with C; decide whether the altruism gene should spread (rB > C) or die out (rB < C).

Work a model case: treat a meerkat sentinel as paying a cost C to warn relatives (benefit B shared among kin). Vary r, B and C and find the threshold where helping becomes favoured. Note that field studies suggest sentinels may face little extra risk and may also benefit themselves (for example, they often spot danger and reach cover first), so real sentinel behaviour may not be pure kin-selected altruism.
Explain why this is a gene's-eye prediction — helping copies of one's own genes carried in relatives — rather than 'for the good of the species'.
activities.intendedInsight: Apparent self-sacrifice toward relatives is a calculable prediction of inclusive fitness: an altruism gene spreads when rB > C. This replaces vague group-benefit reasoning with quantitative individual/gene-level reasoning.

activities.title: Hawk-dove game: no single best move
feedback: If a learner expects pure aggression always to win: with injury cost greater than resource value, have them seed a population of almost all hawks plus a few doves (or add a few dove mutants to an all-hawk population) and watch hawks' average payoff fall as they keep fighting each other; the rare doves then do better than the hawks and increase. A population with no doves at all cannot be invaded by doves until some doves appear. (If injury cost is not greater than resource value the balance shifts toward hawks, so the payoffs matter.)

If a learner expects a single best strategy: point to the stable MIX the population converges on under these payoffs, and show how changing the payoffs moves that mix — or tips it to pure hawk — rather than crowning one fixed winner.

If a learner thinks the equilibrium is set by the starting mix: have them try several different starting mixes that each contain both hawks and doves, keeping the payoffs fixed, and notice they converge toward the same stable proportion.
activities.rationale: A population that the learner seeds and watches converge makes frequency dependence self-evident; live payoff controls let the equilibrium shift under the learner's hand. Reading a matrix alone can assess the idea but does not show the equilibrium settling itself.
sourceClaims: The hawk-dove game illustrates an evolutionarily stable strategy: the best behaviour is frequency-dependent, yielding a stable mix rather than a single winner.
learnerActions: Read a hawk-dove payoff matrix and work out what a hawk and a dove each gain when they meet a hawk and when they meet a dove.

Seed a population with a chosen starting mix of hawks and doves and let it play repeated contests. With the default payoffs set so injury cost exceeds resource value, watch the proportions settle toward a stable mixed equilibrium (the evolutionarily stable strategy).

Change the payoffs (e.g. the cost of injury in a hawk-hawk fight) and observe how the equilibrium moves — a mixed ESS when injury cost exceeds resource value, shifting toward pure hawk when it does not.

With injury cost set higher than the resource value, predict what happens when a few doves are added to a population that is almost all hawks, then test it: explain why pure aggression stops winning once almost everyone is a hawk.
activities.intendedInsight: The best behaviour can be frequency-dependent: with injury cost exceeding resource value an ESS is a stable mix, not a lone winner. 'Survival of the fittest' does not mean the strongest or most aggressive always wins — the best move depends on what everyone else is playing and on the payoff values (with a low injury cost, pure hawk can instead be favoured).

activities.title: Knowledge check: fitness, Hamilton's rule and payoffs
feedback: For a fitness item answered as 'survives longest' or 'strongest': restate fitness as reproductive success and cite the showy short-lived male who out-reproduces a drab survivor.
For an rB-vs-C error: have the learner recompute rB and line it up against C before deciding.
A recognition check confirms recall but does not show whether the learner can explore the trade-offs and equilibria themselves — pair it with the models above.
activities.rationale: A targeted check verifies the computational and definitional pieces that underpin the three models: the definition of fitness, the arithmetic of Hamilton's rule, and reading a payoff matrix. It is a complement to, not a substitute for, operating the models, since it does not elicit exploration of trade-offs or equilibria.
sourceClaims: Sexual selection (female choice, male-male competition, runaway and handicap/honest-signal models) explains costly ornaments; kin selection via Hamilton's rule (rB > C) and inclusive fitness explains altruism toward relatives.
Natural selection acts through differential reproductive success and changes trait distributions over generations.
The hawk-dove game illustrates an evolutionarily stable strategy: the best behaviour is frequency-dependent, yielding a stable mix rather than a single winner.
learnerActions: Answer what 'fittest' means in evolution (reproductive success, not longest survival or greatest strength).
Given r, B and C values, compute rB and state whether rB > C, and hence whether helping is favoured.
Read a hawk-dove payoff matrix and identify which strategy pays better against a given opponent.
activities.intendedInsight: Consolidates the definition of fitness, the arithmetic of Hamilton's rule, and reading a payoff matrix as checkable knowledge.

activities.title: Optional debate: noble meerkat, or Hamilton's rule? (cognitive ethology extension)
feedback: If a learner settles 'nobility' as fact: ask what observation would distinguish a noble motive from a kin-selected one, and whether either is directly measurable.
If a learner accepts an animal-culture claim uncritically: have them separate the behaviour observed from the inferred inner state, and name the evidence needed.
Keep this as discussion: the quantitative models above are best operated, while this extension builds the working-scientifically skill of constructing evidence-based explanations.
activities.rationale: A Socratic debate develops the skill of constructing evidence-based explanations and probes the group-selection misconception, while cognitive ethology is genuinely an evidence/interpretation question suited to discussion. No cited source directly addresses cognitive ethology, so no source claim is mapped here.
learnerActions: Argue the possible explanations for 'is the meerkat sentinel being noble, is it Hamilton's rule, or is it simply looking after itself?' and decide which explanations make testable predictions.
Examine a claim about animal emotion, play or culture and separate the evidence from the interpretation — state what observation would support or weaken the claim.
Challenge a 'for the good of the species' statement and reframe it at the individual/gene level.
activities.intendedInsight: Behavioural explanations must be evidence-based; cognitive-ethology claims about animal emotion or culture are open evidence questions, and group-benefit language can usually be recast in individual/gene-level terms.

constraints: Redefine fitness explicitly as reproductive success (not survival, strength or longevity) before introducing any of the three models, or the peacock's tail stays paradoxical.
Hamilton's rule should be taught with concrete relatedness numbers (e.g. full sibling r = 0.5) so altruism is a quantitative gene's-eye prediction, not a vague appeal to 'the good of the group'.
Actively dismantle 'for the good of the species' group-selection thinking; replace it with individual/gene-level reasoning across all activities.

A static labelled diagram can introduce the ornament trade-off and a quiz can check rB vs C and matrix reading, but neither lets learners locate the net-fitness peak or watch an equilibrium settle; treat them as scaffolds/checks alongside the manipulable models.

The hawk-dove population result depends on the payoff values chosen; the mixed ESS holds when injury cost exceeds resource value, while a low injury cost can favour pure hawk, so avoid teaching one fixed mix as a universal answer.
Cognitive-ethology claims (animal emotion, play, culture) are evidence questions; present them as open and distinguish observation from interpretation rather than asserting conclusions.

Frequency sliders, live-converging populations and payoff-matrix controls are illustrative mechanisms to make the models concrete, not mandatory implementations; equivalent manipulable representations are acceptable.
reviewNotes: This is an agent semantic rewrite of saved teaching research without fresh source verification; all sources[].claim entries remain verified:false and were not re-fetched. Activities are research-informed proposals, not validated interventions.
Bird-of-paradise displays, frog calls and male-male competition were restored to the sexual-selection activity from the source description/claim, having been dropped in an earlier draft.

Self-audit of arithmetic/logic: Hamilton's rule rB > C is stated correctly and the full-sibling r = 0.5 example is standard; the net-fitness peak requires mating benefit to rise faster than survival cost over the relevant range, which the model should ensure. No numerical errors were found in the source to correct.

The source's original artefact ratings asserted a static image 'cannot' carry the models and that 3D 'adds no conceptual value'; these comparative/necessity claims are not established by the cited sources and have been softened to scoped affordance statements (static/quiz as scaffolds and checks).
Runaway vs handicap/honest-signal are presented together as explanations for costly ornaments; these are distinct mechanisms — ensure learners are not told the sim proves one over the other.

The claim that an all-hawk population 'does badly' and the specific stable mix depend on the chosen payoff matrix (injury cost relative to resource value); set payoffs so the ESS is a genuinely mixed outcome before presenting it as such, and note low-cost regimes can favour pure hawk. Hawk-dove learner actions were reworded so the mixed-ESS outcome is stated as a consequence of injury cost exceeding resource value rather than a universal result.

probeDeeper: What does 'fittest' actually mean in evolution — surviving longest, or something else?
Why might a peahen benefit from choosing a male with an outrageously costly tail?
A worker bee is sterile and dies defending the hive. How can 'selfish genes' produce such self-sacrifice?
If being a pure aggressive 'hawk' always won, what would happen once nearly everyone is a hawk?
assess.correctAnswer: Because survival isn't all that counts — evolutionarily what matters is passing on genes, which needs both surviving AND mating. Peahens prefer males with big, showy tails (a costly tail can signal a healthy, high-quality male), so bigger-tailed males mate more and leave more offspring. That extra mating success outweighs the survival cost, so the trait spreads and can even run away to extremes. This is sexual selection — a form of natural selection in which mating advantage, not just survival, drives the trait.

errorPatterns.pattern: Natural selection keeps only traits that aid survival, so a costly tail should be eliminated
errorPatterns.nextMove: Redefine fitness as reproductive success — a trait that lowers survival can still spread if it raises mating success enough.
errorPatterns.distractor: Natural selection should have removed the tail, because it only hurts the peacock's survival.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Predicts the tail should vanish; treats survival as the whole of fitness.

errorPatterns.pattern: The peacock grows a big tail on purpose to attract mates, or because it wants to look good
errorPatterns.nextMove: Recast as selection over generations on heritable variation in tail size via female preference, not an individual's choice.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Frames the tail as a strategy chosen by the individual within its lifetime.

errorPatterns.pattern: Self-sacrifice (a worker bee dying for the hive) evolves 'for the good of the species'
errorPatterns.nextMove: Introduce inclusive fitness and Hamilton's rule — helping close relatives propagates shared genes, so the bee's sacrifice favours copies of its own genes in kin.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Explains altruism as being for the survival of the species as a whole.

errorPatterns.pattern: 'Survival of the fittest' means the strongest or most aggressive individual always wins
errorPatterns.nextMove: Use the hawk-dove model — an all-hawk population does badly; the best strategy is frequency-dependent (an evolutionarily stable strategy).
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Assumes pure aggression is always the best strategy.

responseLevels.gap: Equates fitness with individual survival; says the costly tail should disappear and treats altruism as impossible or simply 'for the good of the species'.
responseLevels.full: Explains fitness as reproductive success, resolves the peacock paradox through a mating-versus-survival trade-off and female choice/signalling (including runaway selection), accounts for altruism via kin selection and inclusive fitness, and recognises that the best behavioural strategy is frequency-dependent (hawk-dove / ESS).
responseLevels.partial: Knows sexual selection favours mating and states 'peahens like big tails', but can't connect it to fitness as reproductive success, and handles altruism and game-theoretic strategy only loosely — listing the ideas without integrating them.

assess.diagnosticPrompt: A peacock's huge, heavy tail makes it slower and easier for predators to catch — it is bad for survival. So why hasn't natural selection got rid of it? Why do peacocks still grow these extravagant tails?
assess.whatMakesItDiscriminate: A student who equates fitness with survival alone says the tail 'should' disappear or can't explain it. A student who understands fitness as reproductive success explains the mating-versus-survival trade-off and names female choice or signalling. Resolving the apparent paradox through reproduction is the discriminator.
